q: The IUPAC name of CH₃COOH is:
x: CH₃COOH has two carbon atoms including the carboxyl carbon, so it is ethanoic acid (acetic acid). Ethanal, CH₃CHO, is an aldehyde.

q: Formic acid, HCOOH, found in ant stings, has the IUPAC name:
x: HCOOH has one carbon atom, so it is methanoic acid. Methanal (HCHO) is an aldehyde and methanol (CH₃OH) is an alcohol.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH (butyric acid) is:
x: The chain has four carbons counting the COOH carbon, so the name is butanoic acid. Counting only the carbons outside COOH wrongly gives propanoic acid.

q: The correct IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)COOH is:
x: The longest chain containing COOH has three carbons (propanoic acid); the COOH carbon is C-1, so the methyl group is on C-2. Counting the methyl carbon into the main chain would give butanoic acid, which is a different isomer.

q: The carbon atom of a carboxyl group (–COOH) is:
o: sp³ hybridised with a tetrahedral arrangement
sp hybridised with a linear arrangement
sp² hybridised with a planar arrangement
x: The carboxyl carbon forms three σ bonds and one π bond (to C=O oxygen), so it is sp² hybridised and the group is planar with angles of about 120°.

q: Ethanoic acid (Mr 60) boils at 118 °C, while propan-1-ol (Mr 60) boils at 97 °C. The main reason is that ethanoic acid:
o: Has a much higher molar mass
x: Two ethanoic acid molecules join by two hydrogen bonds to form a dimer, effectively doubling the particle size and the attractions. Both compounds have the same Mr and both hydrogen bond, but the alcohol forms only single hydrogen bonds.

q: Ethanoic acid can be prepared by heating ethanol under reflux with:
x: Acidified dichromate oxidises a primary alcohol first to the aldehyde and, under reflux, on to the carboxylic acid. Concentrated H₂SO₄ at 170 °C dehydrates ethanol to ethene, and LiAlH₄ is a reducing agent.

q: Heating ethanenitrile, CH₃CN, with dilute acid (acid hydrolysis) gives:
x: CH₃CN + 2H₂O + H⁺ → CH₃COOH + NH₄⁺. The –CN carbon becomes the –COOH carbon, so no carbon is lost or gained. Ethanamine forms by reduction of the nitrile, not hydrolysis.

q: Bromoethane, CH₃CH₂Br, is heated with ethanolic KCN and the product is then hydrolysed with dilute acid. The final organic product is:
x: CH₃CH₂Br + CN⁻ → CH₃CH₂CN, which adds one carbon; hydrolysis gives CH₃CH₂COOH, propanoic acid. Propan-1-amine would need reduction of the nitrile instead of hydrolysis.

q: Methylmagnesium bromide, CH₃MgBr, reacts with carbon dioxide and the product is hydrolysed with dilute acid. The organic product is:
x: The Grignard reagent adds to CO₂ to give CH₃COOMgBr, which on acid hydrolysis gives CH₃COOH. CO₂ supplies the extra carboxyl carbon, so the acid has one more carbon than the Grignard reagent.

q: Which reagent gives effervescence of CO₂ with ethanoic acid but no reaction with ethanol?
x: Carboxylic acids are strong enough to release CO₂ from NaHCO₃; alcohols are not. Sodium and PCl₅ react with both compounds, and acidified dichromate oxidises ethanol.

q: Which of these is the strongest acid?
x: Electron-withdrawing chlorine atoms spread the negative charge of the carboxylate ion and stabilise it; three Cl atoms have the largest effect. Alkyl groups release electrons and weaken the acid.

q: Carboxylic acids are much stronger acids than alcohols mainly because:
o: The carboxylate ion is stabilised by resonance over two oxygen atoms
Carboxylic acids have a higher molar mass
The O–H bond in alcohols is more polar
Alcohols form stronger hydrogen bonds with water
x: In RCOO⁻ the negative charge is delocalised equally over two oxygen atoms, so the ion is stable and forms readily. In an alkoxide ion RO⁻ the charge stays on one oxygen.

q: A 0.1 mol dm⁻³ solution of ethanoic acid conducts electricity less well than 0.1 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid because ethanoic acid:
o: Is a covalent molecule that does not ionise at all
Is only partially ionised in water
x: Ethanoic acid is a weak acid; only a small fraction of molecules ionise, so there are fewer ions to carry current. HCl ionises almost completely. It does ionise a little, so it is not a non-conductor.

q: 0.2 mol of ethanoic acid reacts completely with excess sodium metal. What volume of hydrogen is formed at STP? (1 mol gas = 22.4 dm³)
x: 2CH₃COOH + 2Na → 2CH₃COONa + H₂, so 0.2 mol acid gives 0.1 mol H₂ = 0.1 × 22.4 = 2.24 dm³. Ignoring the 2 : 1 ratio gives 4.48 dm³.

q: Ethanoic acid is reduced by lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH₄) in dry ether, followed by water. The product is:
x: LiAlH₄ reduces –COOH to –CH₂OH, giving the primary alcohol ethanol. Ethanal is an intermediate that is reduced further and is not isolated; the carbon chain is unchanged.

q: Methanoic acid (HCOOH) is a stronger acid than ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) because:
o: The methyl group in ethanoic acid is electron-releasing and destabilises its anion
Methanoic acid has a lower molar mass
Ethanoic acid cannot form a carboxylate ion
Methanoic acid has two O–H groups
x: The CH₃ group pushes electrons towards the carboxylate group, increasing the negative charge and making CH₃COO⁻ less stable. HCOO⁻ has no such group, so methanoic acid ionises more.

q: What mass of sodium hydroxide is needed to neutralise exactly 6.0 g of ethanoic acid? (C 12, H 1, O 16, Na 23)
x: Mr of CH₃COOH = 60, so 6.0 g = 0.1 mol. It reacts 1 : 1 with NaOH (Mr 40): 0.1 × 40 = 4.0 g. Using a 1 : 2 ratio gives 8.0 g.

q: Which shows the correct order of increasing acid strength?
o: Ethanol < phenol < ethanoic acid < chloroethanoic acid
Phenol < ethanol < ethanoic acid < chloroethanoic acid
Ethanol < ethanoic acid < phenol < chloroethanoic acid
Ethanol < phenol < chloroethanoic acid < ethanoic acid
x: Ethanol hardly ionises; the phenoxide ion is stabilised by the ring; carboxylate is stabilised more strongly by resonance over two O atoms; an electron-withdrawing Cl makes chloroethanoic acid stronger still.

q: Ethanoic acid reacts with thionyl chloride, SOCl₂. The organic product is:
x: CH₃COOH + SOCl₂ → CH₃COCl + SO₂ + HCl. The –OH of the acid is replaced by –Cl to give the acyl chloride; the C=O group remains.

q: Thionyl chloride is often preferred to PCl₅ for converting a carboxylic acid into an acyl chloride because:
o: The by-products SO₂ and HCl are gases and escape, leaving a purer product
SOCl₂ does not react with water
SOCl₂ gives a better yield of ester
SOCl₂ does not need the –OH group
x: Both by-products of SOCl₂ are gases, so the acyl chloride is easily separated. With PCl₅ the liquid by-product POCl₃ has to be separated by distillation.

q: In the reaction CH₃COOH + PCl₅ → CH₃COCl + W + HCl, the substance W is:
x: PCl₅ gives the acyl chloride with phosphorus oxychloride and HCl: CH₃COOH + PCl₅ → CH₃COCl + POCl₃ + HCl. H₃PO₃ is the by-product when PCl₃ is used.

q: Ethanoic acid is warmed with ethanol in the presence of a little concentrated H₂SO₄. The organic product is:
x: Acid + alcohol give an ester and water: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O. The ester is named from the alcohol (ethyl) and the acid (ethanoate).

q: In the esterification of ethanoic acid with ethanol, concentrated H₂SO₄:
o: Acts as a catalyst and absorbs water, shifting equilibrium towards the ester
x: Esterification is a slow reversible reaction; H⁺ from H₂SO₄ catalyses it and the acid's dehydrating action removes water, helping the yield of ester.

q: Ethanoic acid is esterified with ethanol in which the oxygen atom is the isotope ¹⁸O (CH₃CH₂¹⁸OH). The ¹⁸O is found in:
o: Both the ester and the water equally
x: In esterification the acid loses its –OH and the alcohol loses only H, so the alcohol oxygen ends up in the ester: CH₃CO¹⁸OC₂H₅. The water's oxygen comes from the acid.

q: Ethanoic acid reacts with ammonia to form a salt. When this salt is heated strongly, the organic product is:
x: CH₃COOH + NH₃ → CH₃COONH₄ (ammonium ethanoate); on heating it loses water: CH₃COONH₄ → CH₃CONH₂ + H₂O, giving ethanamide.

q: Ethanoyl chloride reacts with sodium ethanoate. The organic product is:
x: CH₃COCl + CH₃COONa → (CH₃CO)₂O + NaCl. Two acyl groups joined through an oxygen atom form the acid anhydride.

q: Which is the correct order of decreasing reactivity of carboxylic acid derivatives towards nucleophiles such as water?
o: Acyl chloride > acid anhydride > ester > amide
Ester > amide > acyl chloride > acid anhydride
Acid anhydride > acyl chloride > ester > amide
Amide > ester > acid anhydride > acyl chloride
x: Cl⁻ is the best leaving group, so acyl chlorides react fastest; anhydrides are next, then esters. Amides are least reactive because the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised onto the C=O group.

q: Ethanoyl chloride gives white fumes in moist air because it:
o: Hydrolyses rapidly to ethanoic acid and HCl
Is oxidised by oxygen in the air
Reacts with nitrogen in the air
x: CH₃COCl + H₂O → CH₃COOH + HCl. The HCl gas formed meets moisture and produces steamy white fumes.

q: Ethanamide is formed rapidly at room temperature when ammonia reacts with:
x: CH₃COCl + 2NH₃ → CH₃CONH₂ + NH₄Cl. Chloroethane with ammonia gives an amine (ethylamine), not an amide, and ethanol and ethanal do not give amides.

q: Ethyl ethanoate is heated under reflux with aqueous sodium hydroxide. The products are:
x: Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) goes to completion: CH₃COOC₂H₅ + NaOH → CH₃COONa + C₂H₅OH. The acid appears as its sodium salt because NaOH is present.
